11/16/37
I have just met on the boat one of Dr. Sun's nurses, now working
for the Chinese government. The pleasant-looking one with the nice smile
and beautiful teeth that came over to the house aiter you left the hos-
pital. I showed her the pictures of you and the baby and she asked for
one, so I gave it to her. She seemed very much pleased.
I am now on board the Jardine steamer Kung Wo bound for Hankow,
if it ever shoves off. Just now we are anchored about three miles above
Nanking taking on thousands of refugees. I could not get a seat on our
plane from Wuhu to Hankow until Sunday,
so Max and I decided to make
every effort to get on this although we were told every cabin had been
sold, all deck space, and two hundred on the waiting list, but we decided
to go down early with the head porter of the Metropolitan Hotel and see
what could be done. The boat was due in at 6:30 A.M. and due out at 8.
About nine o'clock
last night Donald called me and wanted to know
what all the trouble with C.N.A.C. was about. I told him I would lake
to tell him about it but would li have to see him. He said it was entire -
ly impossible to
see him that night but he could see me in the morning.
I rushed down to the hotel and saw Max and told him I probably could not
go with him unless the
boat left as late as noon as I was going to stay
over to see Donald, but I told him to get me a cabin anyway if possible
and pay for it, just in case the boat should be late.
I saw Don at 9:30 and had a very friendly and interesting talk
with him. He promised
to go to bat for us. I gave him a short memoran-
dum of what we wanted and told him we would not consider anything less.
One of them was the removal of Aviation Commission officials as exec-
utives in our company.
I recommended P.Y. as M.D. - but any business
man. Right now it looks to me as if China is on the verge of a complete
collapse so I am afraid neither Don nor any one else is going to be
able to accomplish anything constructive. I hear from excellent sources,
Chinese,
the Government is going to move to Changsha and Hankow.
There is starting now just the beginning of an evacuation of Nanking
which seems to me to be gaining velocity by leaps and bounds and may
soon become a panic. So anything can happen, and I keep my fingers ea
crossed. After leaving Don I rushed back to Sidney's, got my suitcase,
beat it
to the Bund to the China Travel Office. I learned my boat
had not s ailed, was still three miles up the river, but no one knew
when it was going to sail or how I could get there.
I ran into Dr. Lee from Wusih. He seemed like a lost soul, said
his hospital in Wusih had been bombed,his house is next to it, his
family were in Shanghai, he couldn't get transportation in either dir-
ection. He wanted to go
to Shanghai but understood the trip down the
river and around the blockade was impossible. His son-in-law was with
him. I asked him if he had lost his hospital. He said,"I have lost
everything". I asked him if he had any reason for staying in Nanking.
He said he did not as he could do nothing there, that he wanted to go
to Shanghai as his daughter was having a baby next month.Neither of
them, he or his son-in-law seemed capable of making any decision. I
him I had just come up from Shanghai under the most adverse con-
ditions and considered the trip perfectly all right but a little uncom-
fortable. He wanted to know the best way to do it. I told him to take
the first steamer to Kowan on the upper side of the blockade, go ashore
at once and find out the places from which small boats left. To take the
first boat leaving, no matter what, it was, and stay on it until he hac
a chance to transfer to a better one, but to keep moving in the direc-
tion of Nantung. If he had luck he would make it in arouna 20 hours,
nee-&*-Hentang but in any case he should get around in 48 hours. Once
